text:
The fluorescent hum of Aisle 4 was the only soundtrack. Mrs. Gable stood frozen, a tin of crushed tomatoes hovering mid-air, her knuckles white against the cold metal. Across the cart, Leo—once the boy who whispered poetry during detention—now wore a coat that smelled of rain and expensive coffee. Twenty years had carved lines into his face, yet his eyes held that same restless curiosity.

"Mr. Vance," she said, the title slipping out like a rehearsed line.

He flinched, then smiled, a slow, disarming curve. "Just Leo, Mrs. Gable. And you’re… still teaching?"

"No," she replied, placing the tomato in her basket with deliberate care. "I’m buying dinner."

The silence stretched, thick with unsaid apologies and ungranted forgivenesses. He reached for a loaf of bread; she adjusted her scarf. They were strangers bound by a ghost classroom, separated by the mundane geography of produce and dairy.

"I remember your essay on Keats," he said softly.

"I remember you crying over it," she countered, though her voice lacked its old edge.

They nodded, a mutual acknowledgment of time’s indifferent passage. As their carts diverged, wheeling toward checkout lanes numbered four and five, neither looked back. The supermarket continued its rhythmic pulse, swallowing them whole, leaving only the echo of a bell from a distant register.
